manifest.title: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration.
manifest.summary: A ball tossed straight up and a second ball held by a gate at the top, shown side by side with velocity and acceleration arrows. The gate opens at the top, and from then on both balls move together.
assumptions: No air resistance, the same gravity for both balls, up is positive.
An idealized vertical throw; real balls feel drag.
manifest.description: Two side-by-side lanes share a height scale from 0 to 2.2 m above the launch mark. On the left, a blue Toss lane shows a ball thrown up and falling back. On the right, a gold Drop lane shows a ball held by a gate at the top height until the toss reaches the top. Each ball has a solid velocity arrow, a dashed acceleration arrow and a callout with v and a.

plan.title: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration.
plan.story:
Maya tossed the ball straight up, waited for it to hang at the top, and swung. By then it had dropped below her racket.

"I don't get it," she said. "If it stopped, how was it still accelerating?"

Her friend picked up the ball and held it at shoulder height. "Watch what happens the moment I let go."

He opened his fingers. The ball began to fall. It started with zero velocity, and gravity immediately began giving it downward speed.

Maya looked up. Her own ball had passed through that same moment. The difference was how it got there. Her hand had sent it upward, and gravity had been slowing its climb from the moment it left her fingers.

She pictured three instants around the top. A tenth of a second before, it was moving up at about a metre per second. At the top, its velocity was zero. A tenth of a second later, it was moving down at about a metre per second.

Velocity tells you how fast something is moving and which way. Acceleration tells you how quickly that velocity changes. In each tenth of a second, the ball's velocity changed by about one metre per second downward. Zero was one of the values it passed through.

Maya took another ball. She began her swing while it was still climbing and met it as it came down. This one cleared the net.
plan.cardDescription: At the top, velocity is zero for an instant, but gravity keeps changing it: a = -g. A gate releases a second ball at that moment. No air resistance.
plan.learningGoal: Explain why the acceleration is not zero at the top, where the velocity is zero, by comparing the tossed ball with a ball released from rest.
plan.instructions: Change launch speed or gravity, then press Play. At each pause, compare velocity and acceleration. Press Play again to continue, or drag the timeline. At top jumps to the shared release.

scene.description: Two equal-width lanes side by side in one frame: a blue Toss lane and a gold Drop lane, each with a heading and a state line (Toss: At launch, Rising, At the top, Falling, At launch height; Drop: Held in place, Just released, Falling together, At launch height). Both use the same fixed 0 to 2.2 m height scale and the same velocity-arrow and acceleration-arrow scales; zero height is the launch mark, up is positive. A release gate at the apex height holds the second ball (velocity and acceleration zero) until the top, then opens. Each ball has a blue velocity arrow on one side and a dashed warm acceleration arrow on the other, and a callout of two readings: v in m/s and a in m/s^2. After release faint outlines keep the shared starting height. No graph, no mass control, no snapshot strip.

observations.text: The toss velocity reads +0.98, 0.00 and -0.98 m/s at -0.10, 0 and +0.10 s from the top at 9.8 m/s^2.
The toss acceleration stays at -gravity (-9.8 m/s^2 by default) at every instant, including the top.
After the release the dropped ball has the same height, velocity and acceleration as the tossed ball at every shared instant.
A faster toss or a weaker gravity moves the top later and higher; the readings at the top do not change.

findings.message: At launch the drop ball is held at apex height 0.816 m, but the drawn y is 240.9 with scale 240px/2.2m from baseline 330. That gives about 89 px of height, so it is drawn correctly. The problem is the tossed ball's velocity arrow at t=0. It runs from 330 to 274, which is 56 px for 4 m/s, or 14 px per m/s. At cp-before, 0.98 m/s gives 13.7 px, so the scale is consistent. Even so, the toss lane has no 'Held' state at the start, and the Toss lane state line at the top is the same as the plan says, so this is not an error.

At the top the drop ball's acceleration reads -9.8 while its state says 'Just released'. Before the top it reads 0 while held. This matches the plan. But the drop ball's acceleration jumps from 0 to -g at the instant the velocity is zero, and the card gives no explanation. The card's claim is that both balls share acceleration at every instant after release. Drop acceleration at cp-before is 0, so the claim 'toss acceleration is -gravity throughout' holds, but the readouts for cp-before show the pair disagreeing. This is acceptable only if the scene says why.

The fast-toss apex height is 2.083 m. The drawn y is 102.7 on a 240 px / 2.2 m scale, which gives 330-227=103, so it is consistent. However, the time reading cannot be verified: the scrubber range and the 'Time from the top' offset are not shown in the frames. The scrubber and the control effects (At top seek, reset, speed and gravity) cannot be judged from these frames and traces.
The lane title and state text share y=16, with the state at x=160 and the title at x=80. Whether they overlap cannot be judged without pixels.
